implementation_notes: C has neither inheritance nor an ORM, so the hierarchy is flattened into one struct per table row (or one struct with a union for the subtype fields) plus a kind field holding the discriminator, and a hand-written mapper switches on that kind to build the matching concrete value. The table side is written with prepared statements (sqlite3_prepare_v2/bind/step or libpq); since SQLite does not type-check columns, only explicit CHECK constraints can connect the tag to the columns it requires, so the discipline lives half in code and half in the schema. Choose this shape while the subtypes stay few and share most fields; hand-written tables per subtype are clearer once they diverge.
pitfalls: An unknown or stale tag must fail loudly: without a default arm that reports the value, the mapper returns a half-initialised object and the drift only shows up as wrong behaviour later.

Nothing in a C struct ties the tag to the populated fields, so rows can hold columns belonging to another subtype; a CHECK constraint (type <> 'manager' OR reports IS NOT NULL) is the only guard the database offers.
Column order and types in the struct must match the SELECT list exactly - C has no reflection, so schema changes are silent until values land in the wrong fields.
